transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Yeah, thank you for seeing me. I'm just... well, I came in today because I feel completely worn out all the time. And I mean all the time. It doesn't even seem to matter what I do or how much rest I get. I'll go to bed, get a full night's sleep—sometimes eight or nine hours, which usually would be plenty for me—but when my alarm goes off, it's like my body is made of sandbags. Just absolute dead weight. 

I work as a market research analyst, so I really need my brain to be sharp, looking at data and trends all day, but getting through a single workday right now feels almost impossible. I just sit at my desk feeling like I'm moving through wet concrete. And it's not even just the big things like work. It's the stupid, mundane stuff at home, too. Like folding laundry. I'll manage to get the clothes washed and dried, but then they just sit in the basket for a week because the actual physical act of picking up a towel and folding it takes absolutely everything I have. Every ounce of energy. I just don't understand why I'm so drained, but it's really starting to impact every single part of my day.
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or have you lost interest or pleasure in things that used to bring you joy?

Yeah, I... I definitely have. It's actually—well, it's hard to separate it from the exhaustion sometimes, but it's definitely there. It's more than just being tired, you know? It's like... most days, I wake up, and before I even get out of bed, before my feet even touch the floor, I have this heavy, just completely flat feeling sitting right in the middle of my chest. It physically weighs me down. 

I'll drag myself out to the kitchen, maybe pour a cup of coffee that I don't even really want to drink, and I'll just sit at the kitchen table. We have this big window that looks out over the back yard, and I can sit there staring at the yard, looking at the grass or the fence, for God knows how long. Just staring. And while I'm sitting there, my brain just starts going to these incredibly empty places. I'll sit there and just feel like... like there is absolutely no good version of the future coming. None at all. 

I try to logic my way out of it sometimes. You know, in my job, I analyze data, I look for positive trends, I try to forecast things based on evidence. But when it comes to my own life right now, I look ahead and it's just a blank wall. I can't picture anything good happening, or anything getting easier, or me ever snapping out of this. It's just this overwhelming certainty that this flat, heavy existence is all that's left, and I just sit at that table letting my coffee go completely cold because I can't even find the motivation to take a sip, let alone care about any of the hobbies or things I used to actually enjoy doing. It just all feels so pointless.
Have you had any thoughts about ending your life or that life isn't worth living?

I... well, I wouldn't say I want to end my life, exactly. Not like I'm sitting down and figuring out how to do it. But... the thoughts are there. They sneak up on me. It usually happens late at night, when the house is totally quiet. My husband, Dave, he works construction, so he's usually asleep by 9:30, completely out. And I'll just be lying there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, listening to him breathe. And my brain just starts spinning. 

I start thinking about how much of a drag I've been lately, how I barely talk at dinner, how I haven't helped with the yard work in months. And then this thought just... slides into my head. This really quiet, persistent thought that maybe Dave would just be better off if I wasn't here. If he didn't have to deal with this heavy, exhausted version of me. I'll lay there and almost convince myself that it would be a relief for him. Like taking a heavy backpack off after a long hike. 

And I haven't... I haven't done anything about it. I haven't made a plan or looked anything up or anything like that. I know that's what people always ask. But the fact that the thought keeps coming back, night after night, just sitting there in the dark with me... it really scares me. It scares me that my brain even goes there so easily now, like it's a perfectly logical conclusion to draw from all this data, you know? It's just... it's a really dark place to be stuck in at 2 in the morning.
Have you ever experienced a period like this before, where you felt this level of exhaustion and hopelessness, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

I don't know if I've ever felt it quite this bad before, honestly. I mean, everyone gets tired, and I've definitely had periods where work was stressful and I felt burnt out, but this current stretch... this depressed, slowed-down, completely exhausted part... it's been going on most days for about the past two months now. 

I know it's been about two months because I remember right around the end of October, we were gearing up for all the end-of-year forecasting at work. Usually, that's a busy time, lots of data sets to clean and trend lines to build, and normally I just put on my headphones, drink my coffee, and power through it. But this year, right around then, I just hit this absolute wall. I remember staring at my monitors, looking at a spreadsheet template I've used a hundred times, and it was like my brain was just wading through mud. I couldn't process it. And ever since that week, it's just been this constant, day-in, day-out slog. 

I kept trying to brush it off at first. I kept telling myself, oh, it's just a phase, you're just staring at screens too much, maybe you just need to catch up on your sleep over the weekend. Dave even suggested we just take a couple of days and drive up to his brother's place to unplug, thinking maybe I just needed a change of scenery. But I knew a weekend trip wasn't going to fix it, because it's not just a normal kind of tired. It's like someone threw this thick, heavy wool blanket over my entire life about eight weeks ago and just left it there, and I've been suffocating under it almost every single day since.
Have you ever had a period in the past where you felt this level of depression, or is this the first time you've experienced something this intense?

I... well, I thought I just answered that? I mean, I guess I was talking more about how long this current stretch has been going on, the two months since October. But as for the past... no, I really don't think I've ever had a period quite like this before. 

I've always been a pretty steady person, you know? In my line of work, doing market research and analyzing data, you have to be level-headed. You can't let your emotions dictate how you interpret the numbers. And I've always applied that to my own life, too. If I felt stressed, I'd step back, look at the variables, and figure out a solution. Like, a few years ago, we were doing this massive consumer behavior study for a new client, and the deadline was insane. I was working 60-hour weeks, and I definitely felt burnt out. I was tired, I was cranky, I snapped at Dave a few times over stupid things like loading the dishwasher wrong. But even then, even when I was totally exhausted from the sheer volume of work, I never felt this... this profound emptiness. I never sat at the kitchen table staring at the fence feeling like the future was a black hole. 

So, yeah, I've had stressful times, and I've had periods where I just wanted to sleep for a week, but it was always tied to something tangible, like a project deadline or a busy season at work. Once the project was done, I bounced back. I'd take a weekend off, maybe do some gardening, and I'd feel like myself again. But this... this is entirely different. This isn't just bouncing back from a hard week. This feels like my baseline has completely shifted, and I've never experienced anything this intense or this heavy in my entire life. It's really uncharted territory for me, which I guess is why it's so terrifying. I don't have any past data to look at to tell me how to get out of it.
Have you ever experienced a period of depression before that was serious enough that you sought help or received treatment for it?

No, no, never. Like I was just saying, this whole... this whole experience is completely new to me. I've never been to a psychiatrist before, or a therapist, or anyone like that for my mental health. I've never even brought up feeling sad or tired to my primary care doctor, Dr. Evans. I've seen him for, gosh, probably fifteen years now, ever since Dave and I moved to this side of town, and the most we ever talk about is my cholesterol—which is fine, by the way, I keep an eye on it—or maybe getting a flu shot in the fall. 

I've just never been the kind of person who needed that kind of help. I always prided myself on being self-sufficient, you know? Like I said, I analyze things for a living. If there was a problem, I fixed it. I didn't need to sit on a couch and talk about my feelings because my feelings never got in the way of my life like this before. Even when my mom passed away about six years ago—which was incredibly sad, of course, she had been sick for a while, but it still hits you hard—I grieved, I cried, I helped my sister sort out the estate, but I didn't fall into a hole. I kept going to work, I kept the house running. I was sad, but it was a normal, manageable kind of sad. 

So, no, I've never sought treatment for depression, I've never taken any kind of medication for it, nothing like that. I wouldn't even know where to begin, honestly. When Dave finally convinced me I needed to talk to someone about what's been happening these last two months, I had to ask Dr. Evans for a referral because I didn't even know how the process worked. It feels very strange to be sitting here, to be honest. I keep thinking there must be some kind of mistake, that I should just be able to snap out of it like I always have, but... I just can't. So, yeah, this is my very first time ever trying to get professional help for anything like this.

Have you ever had a period in your life when you felt down or depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks, to the point where it affected your work, relationships, or other important areas of your life?

Well, like I was saying, never in the past. Never before this current stretch that started back in October. But if you're asking about right now, these last eight weeks or so? Yes, absolutely. It is completely spilling over into every part of my life, which is just so frustrating because I'm usually such an organized, on-top-of-things kind of person. 

At work, for instance, I have actually fallen behind on my client reports. And I have never missed a deadline in my life. I have this one major account, a regional retail chain, and they expect their quarterly trend analysis by the fifteenth of the month. Usually, I have it proofed and in their inbox by the twelfth. But this time, I just couldn't do it. I couldn't get the draft together, I couldn't focus on the numbers, and I ended up having to ask my manager for an extension, which was incredibly embarrassing. 

And it's not just the job, it's my personal life, too. I've started avoiding my friends completely. A couple of my girlfriends, Sarah and Jen, we usually get together for dinner or just grab coffee every other week to catch up, but I've canceled on them three times in a row now. I just make up some excuse about being busy because I can't muster the energy to sit at a restaurant and try to hold a normal conversation. I just don't have it in me. 

I've even stopped doing my outdoor routines, which is probably making things worse, honestly. I usually love being outside—whether it's tending to the garden like I mentioned earlier, or just taking my long morning walks around the neighborhood. Those routines are usually what keep me steady and clear my head before I sit down at my desk for the day. But I haven't put on my walking shoes in weeks. I just look out the window and the thought of even stepping off the porch feels like climbing a mountain. 

So, really, it feels like every single ounce of my energy—what little I even have left right now—just goes into barely getting through work so I don't get fired, and managing the absolute basics at home. You know, making sure the bills are paid and maybe throwing a frozen pizza in the oven so Dave and I have something to eat. That's it. That is my entire capacity right now. So, yes, it's definitely affecting my life, just... only this time, right now. Never before this.
Have you ever had a period in your life, before this current one, where you felt down or depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

I know I keep saying this, but no, never before October. Never in my whole life before these last two months. I've never had a two-week stretch of feeling anything close to this. But during this current period? Yes, it is literally every single day. 

I mean, most days I wake up and before I even get out of bed, before my feet even hit the floor, I have this... this heavy, flat feeling right here in the center of my chest. It’s like a physical weight, but it’s completely hollow at the same time, if that makes any sense at all. I'll drag myself up, pour a cup of coffee that I don't even really want, and I just sit there at the kitchen table. I'll sit there while the coffee goes completely cold, just staring out at the yard. I look out at the grass and the garden beds I haven't touched, and I just feel like... like there is absolutely no good version of the future coming. 

It’s just this incredibly bleak, dark outlook that I cannot shake, no matter how hard I try to rationalize it. In the past, if I had a bad day or a stressful week, I’d look forward to the weekend, or a vacation, or just the relief of finishing a big data set. There was always some sort of light at the end of the tunnel, something good to anticipate. But this feeling I have right now, sitting at that table every morning... it’s like the tunnel just completely collapsed in on me. I can't see anything getting better. So, to answer your question, no, I never had a two-week period like this before the fall, because if I had, I know I would have remembered waking up with this exact, horrible feeling. It's impossible to forget.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current episode—lasting at least two weeks—where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things nearly every day, even if it wasn’t as severe as what you’re experiencing now?

I know we keep circling back to the past, but I really have to emphasize that before this fall, no, absolutely not. I was always so engaged with my life. I never had a period where I just stopped caring about things. But if we're talking about right now, with this current situation... yes, the loss of interest is just staggering. 

I mean, I used to make time for so many things outside of work. Because when you analyze data all day, you really need that mental break, you know? I had my regular yoga classes, I went hiking on the weekends, I spent hours in my garden—like I mentioned before—and I was huge into taking bird photos. My husband Dave bought me this incredible telephoto lens a few years ago, and I used to go down to the nature preserve just a few miles from our house on Saturday mornings. I'd sit there in the quiet and just wait for the perfect shot of a heron or a woodpecker. It brought me so much joy, and I prided myself on making the time for it, no matter how busy work got.

But lately? Since October? I just keep canceling everything. I haven't been to a single yoga class in two months. I let my membership freeze. And my camera is literally just sitting in its case in the hall closet collecting dust. Dave even suggested we go out to the preserve last weekend because the weather was unseasonably warm and sunny, and I just couldn't do it. I couldn't even bring myself to say maybe. None of it feels worth the effort anymore. The thought of packing the camera bag, or putting on my hiking boots, or even just rolling out a yoga mat in the living room... it all just feels so unbelievably pointless and exhausting. Why bother? It’s like all the color has just drained out of the things I used to love, and I can't find a single reason to even try to do them anymore. It's just so unlike me.

Before this current period that started in October, have you ever had a time when you felt down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks in a row, even if it wasn’t as bad as what you're going through now?

I know it probably seems like I'm just repeating myself, and I feel like a bit of a broken record here, but I really, truly have to say no. Not even a milder version of it. I know you have to be thorough, and you're trying to figure out if there's some kind of pattern here or if this has been bubbling under the surface for years, but I promise you, it hasn't. 

I'm 43 years old, and for 42 and a half of those years, I was completely steady. I was always the upbeat one! I mean, sure, everyone has a bad day here and there. You get a flat tire, or a client gets irritated because the market data doesn't say what they want it to say—which happens way more often than you'd think in my line of work, let me tell you—and you feel bummed out for an afternoon. That’s just life. But by the next morning? I was always fine. I'd bounce right back. I'd go for my morning walk, I'd get my coffee, and I was back at it with a smile on my face. 

There was never, ever a time in my past where a bad mood just... stuck to me for weeks on end. It just didn't happen. If I had ever felt even a fraction of this, even for just a few days, let alone two whole weeks, I would have noticed. My husband Dave definitely would have noticed, because it is just so completely opposite to how I usually operate. I was always the one organizing things, keeping everyone's spirits up. So this whole thing, this heavy dark cloud or whatever you want to call it, it really just rolled in completely out of nowhere this fall. So, to answer your question again, no. Absolutely nothing like this, not even a little bit, before October.
Before this current episode that started in October, have you ever had a time when you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks in a row?

I... wait, I feel like we’re going in circles a bit here, Doctor. I really don't mean to be difficult, but the answer is definitely still no. I promise you, I’m not hiding anything from my past. I keep trying to think about why you're asking me this so many times, and I guess... well, I guess it’s because people probably don't usually just wake up one day in October and feel like the bottom completely dropped out of their world without some sort of warning sign first, right? 

And I get that. I really do. As a market research analyst, if I saw a sudden, massive drop-off in a trend line without any prior fluctuations or warning signs in the data, I’d absolutely question it. I’d go back and look for anomalies in the previous quarters, I'd double-check all the variables, I'd make sure nothing was missed. So I completely understand why you're digging into my past like this. You have to be thorough. But my personal data, my history before this fall... it’s just completely steady. There are no two-week dips. Not even a one-week dip. 

Dave and I were actually just talking about this the other night, sitting in the living room, because I've been trying so hard to figure out where this all came from. I literally asked him, "Dave, have I ever been like this before? Did I miss something?" And he just looked at me like I had two heads. He told me I've always been the engine of the house, the one who keeps everything moving and plans all our weekend trips and keeps us social. If I had ever spent two whole weeks feeling down, or if I had stopped caring about my photography or my garden for that long before this October, we both would have a very clear memory of it. It would have been a major event for us. So, no, I just... I never experienced anything like this before.

Before this current episode that started in October, have you ever had a period of time—lasting at least two weeks—where you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day, even if it wasn’t as severe as what you’re experiencing now?

Okay, I really don't want to be rude, Doctor, but did I misunderstand the question the last three times? Or are you required to ask this a certain number of times for insurance purposes? Because I know in market research, sometimes we use repetitive questioning to test response reliability, you know, to see if the respondent changes their answer if you word it just slightly differently. If that's what you're doing, I can assure you, my answer is going to stay exactly the same. 

No. Never. Not once. 

I've literally been racking my brain while we've been talking, going all the way back to my twenties when I was getting my associate's degree, just thinking, "Did I have a slump back then? Did I spend a month in bed when I broke up with my college boyfriend? Did I lose interest in things when I was stressed about finals?" And the answer is still no. Even back then, I was always the one who just kept pushing forward. I'd maybe cry for an evening and then go right back to organizing a study group the next morning. 

There has never been a two-week period—not even a mild one, not even a "feeling a little blue" phase—before this October. I am absolutely, one hundred percent positive. I don't know what else I can say to convince you that this current situation is entirely new for me, but I really have never experienced anything like this before this fall.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current episode when you felt so down or lost interest in things almost every day for at least two weeks, even if it wasn’t as intense as what you're going through now?

Doctor, I... okay. I feel like I'm in some sort of psychological focus group right now, or like I'm being cross-examined. I know I talk a lot, and maybe I buried the lead in my last three answers because I tend to over-explain things, but the answer is still, unequivocally, no. 

I mean, I'm sitting here trying to think if there's *any* possible way I could be misremembering my own life just to give you the answer you seem to be looking for. Like, did I have a bad month in 2015? Did I stop caring about my hobbies back in, I don't know, 2019 when they restructured my department at work? But no, I really didn't. Even when they laid off half my team and I had to take on all the demographic coding myself—which was an absolute nightmare, by the way, just staring at spreadsheets and consumer behavior metrics for days and days—I was still completely fine. I was stressed, sure, maybe a little burnt out, but I wasn't *down*. I didn't lose interest in my life. I was still getting up at 6 AM, still making Dave his lunches, still going to my Thursday night book club, still doing my photography on the weekends. 

I just... I don't know how to make it any clearer, or what else I can pull from my memory to prove it. Before October, before this whole current heavy feeling started, there was never a two-week stretch where I felt down or lost interest. Not even a mild one. I've always been the energetic one, the doer. Always. Until this fall.

Have you ever had a time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things for several days in a row, even if it didn’t last as long as two weeks or wasn’t as intense as what you’re experiencing now?

Ah, okay. So we're changing the parameters a bit. Moving from a two-week trend line down to just a few days. I see what you're doing. But... well, honestly, Doctor, the data still says no. 

Even for just three or four days? Still no. I mean, obviously, I’m a human being, so I’ve had a bad afternoon here and there. Like, if a major focus group recruitment falls through at the last minute or a client completely rejects a quarterly report I spent weeks compiling, sure, I might be cranky for an evening. I might go home, complain to Dave, maybe have a glass of wine and just want to veg out on the couch instead of working on my garden or editing my photos. But waking up the next day, and the day after that, and the day after *that*, just feeling persistently down and not caring about my life? No. Never. 

I've always bounced right back. Dave jokes that I have the emotional resilience of a rubber band, because I just snap right back into place the next morning. If I had lost interest in my life for even a long weekend, that would have been a glaring anomaly. I'm usually the one dragging everyone out of the house on a Saturday morning to go to the farmer's market, or to test out a new macro lens for my camera, or just finding some new household project to tackle. I don't do "down days." I really don't. 

So, no, not even for several days. This whole... whatever this is that started in October, this heavy, awful feeling where I just can't bring myself to care about anything at all, it's completely unprecedented for me. I really don't have a history of this, not for weeks, and not for days. I just don't.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current episode when you had several symptoms of depression—like feeling down, losing interest in things, or having trouble sleeping or eating—for at least two weeks in a row?

Doctor, I feel like we are just slicing the same data set into different demographics at this point. It’s like when we ask consumers if they like a product, and then we ask if they enjoy using the product, and then we ask if the product brings them satisfaction. It’s the same question! 

But to answer you—again—no. Not even if we bundle the symptoms together. I didn't have a two-week period where I felt down *and* stopped eating *and* couldn't sleep. Honestly, before October, my sleep was like clockwork. I’d be in bed by 10:30, asleep by 10:45, up at 6:00, ready to go. And eating? I love to cook. I’ve always loved meal prepping on Sundays, making sure Dave and I have healthy lunches for the week. I never lost my appetite, I never had trouble sleeping, I never felt down, I never lost interest. 

I’m really trying to be helpful here, I promise I am, but I feel like I keep giving you the same answer and you keep waiting for a different one. I’ve never had an episode like this before. Never had the symptoms, not individually, not grouped together, not for two weeks, not for three days. It’s all just a big, definitive zero until this fall. I really don’t know how else to phrase it.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current episode when you had a period of feeling down nearly every day along with a loss of interest in things, lasting at least two weeks?

Doctor, I... okay. Look, I feel like we're just spinning our wheels here, going over the same exact metrics but just changing the wording on the survey. I know you have to ask these things, and I know I probably talk too much and give you way more context than you need, but I just... I don't know how to give you a different answer than the one I've been giving you for the last ten minutes. 

No. I have never, ever, in my entire forty-three years of life, had a two-week period where I felt down every day and lost interest in things. Not before this current situation started in October. 

I mean, I'm sitting here racking my brain, trying to think if maybe I'm just blocking something out. Like, did I have a rough patch when Dave and I first moved in together and we were arguing about how to organize the kitchen? No, that was annoying, but I wasn't depressed. Did I lose interest in things when I had that horrible flu back in 2018? Well, sure, for like five days I didn't want to do anything but sleep and drink ginger ale, but that was a virus, not my mood, and the second my fever broke I was right back to organizing my pantry and planning my weekend photography trip. 

I just... I've always been the upbeat one. The one who makes the spreadsheets for the family vacations and forces everyone to go on a hike at 8 AM. The idea of me just sitting around, feeling down, not caring about my garden or my book club or my job... it's just not me. Or, at least, it wasn't me until this fall. So, no. No two weeks of feeling down and losing interest. Never. Not before now. I really, truly mean it.
Have you ever had a time in your life before this current episode when you felt down or lost interest in things almost every day for at least two weeks in a row?

Okay, Doctor, I... I really have to ask, is this a standard interview technique? Like, asking the exact same question four different ways to see if my answer changes? Because in my line of work, we call that a trap question to weed out bad survey respondents. We use it to make sure people are actually reading the prompts and not just clicking through. But I promise you, my data is clean. I am paying attention, and the answer is still no. Absolutely not. 

I have never, not once in my life before this October, felt down or lost interest in my life for two weeks in a row. 

I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here, just repeating myself over and over! But I really want to be thorough for you, I do. It’s just... if I had spent two weeks feeling down, Dave would have marched me to a doctor himself years ago. We've been together a long time and he's used to me being a total whirlwind of activity. I'm the one who plans the neighborhood block party, who color-codes the recycling bins, who stays up late analyzing focus group transcripts because I just genuinely love finding the patterns in the data. I mean, just last summer, I spent three straight weeks building a custom cedar raised bed for my heirloom tomatoes, out there with a power drill every single evening after working a full nine-to-five. 

Does that sound like someone who loses interest in things for weeks at a time? No. I’ve just always been highly motivated and engaged with my life. So, again, and I really, really hope this is the last time we need to cover this specific metric... no. Never for two weeks. Not before October.
